new_statements.translation: fn.11: Newman's Proto-Chadic *hl (voiceless lateral fricative) is written IPA *ɬ here for readability, e.g. item 1 'to answer' *hləwə > *ɬəwə. High tone is marked (á), low tone (à). [...] fn.15: Owing to the limitations of the data (especially for Gvoko), tone marking has been omitted in the morpho-syntactic example sentences.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: KCI record ART001785761 re-downloaded (citation_title 'Linguistic Features of Dghwede, Guduf and Gvoko..', J. Korean Assoc. of African Studies 38(1):31-66, 2013; download markers present) and Glottolog ref 587981 carries the same Korean title_original with language code Gvoko [ngs]; held PDF is 36 pp. Quote checked in : fn.11 at printed p.39 (p.9, lines 324-328) reads '11) 뉴먼이 차딕 조어에서 재구한 *hl(무성설측마찰음)은.. IPA *ɬ로 통일하였음: 예) 1번 to answer *hləwə > *ɬəwə. 고성조는 (/á/), 저성조는 (/à/) 표시함.' and fn.15 at printed p.47 (p.17, line 737) reads '15) 자료의 한계(특히 그보코어)로 본 형태-통사적 예문에서는 성조 표기를 생략하였음.' -- verbatim apart from extracted textbreaks. I read sections 2-4.2 and the conclusion: data are the author's own 1…
new_statements.relation_note: H/L tone marks on Gvoko words throughout the list (e.g. láɣè 'bow', kə̀là 'break', úzà 'blood'); sound-change section 4.2 is segmental only (*r > l etc.); notes Gvoko-specific final vowel [o].
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author transcribes his first-hand Gvoko lexical data with a two-way tone marking (high á vs low à), i.e. treats Gvoko (like Dghwede and Guduf) as a tone language with at least H and L; tone is left unmarked in the sentence examples for lack of reliable data, especially for Gvoko. No analysis of the tonal system (number of contrastive tones, downstep, functional load) and nothing at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; tone marks omitted in section 4.3 examples (fn.15)
new_statements.identity_note: Gvoko [ngs] of the Gwoza area, NE Nigeria, treated alongside Dghwede and Guduf (Mandara group); data from the author's own fieldwork in Gwoza in 1999 and 2001 (650-word lists, questionnaire sentences, audio) -- fn.9; author states Gvoko had no prior study at all (p.37).

sources.citation: Gravina, Richard. 2014. The Phonology of Proto-Central Chadic. Utrecht: LOT (LOT Dissertation Series 375). 437 pp.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Nothing on Gvoko stress. The source table (p.13) lists Gvoko's data source as 'none'; p.193: 'Dghwede is the only one of the four languages in its subgroup for which we have access to data. Data from Gvoko, Guduf or Cineni would help..'. Only Gvoko data in the book are two lexical items ('nose' xtor, 'ear' ɬuwo, p.78, from Wolff). The book explicitly excludes tone and stress from its reconstruction (p.xxii/ch.1).

sources.citation: Wolff, H. Ekkehard. 2008. Issues in the Historical Phonology of Chadic Languages. Course materials (81 slides/pages), Leipzig Spring School on Linguistic Diversity, Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig, March 2008.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Gvoko appears only in vowel-correspondence tables (slide p.53 'Prosodies & reconstruction (3)': Gvoko 'nose' xtor, 'ear' uwo; repeated pp.75-76 with prosody labels LAB/PAL). Stress is raised only as open questions for Central Chadic in general (p.29: are short non-low vowels 'phonetic reductions of full vocoids.. possibly in unstressed syllables?'; are long vowels 'manifestations of stress?'; p.77: long *ii/*uu 'largely predictable, including realisation of [stress]'). Tone is mentioned only for Hausa verb tone-melody classes (p.8). No statement on Gvoko tone or word stress.
